label: z23
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{z23}   
    Let $\lambda$ be inaccessible, $\bar\theta = 
    \langle \theta_\varepsilon:\varepsilon
    < \lambda\rangle$ be a sequence of regular cardinals $< \lambda$ satisfying $\theta_\varepsilon > \varepsilon$.
    
    1) We define the forcing notion ${\mathbb Q} = {\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}$ by:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(\alpha)$]  $p \in {\mathbb Q}$ \underline{iff}:          
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)]  $p = (\eta,f) = (\eta^p,f^p)$, 
            
            \item[(b)]  $\eta \in \prod\limits_{\zeta < \varepsilon} \theta_\zeta$ for some $\varepsilon < \lambda$, ($\eta$ is called the trunk of $p$), 
            
            \item[(c)] $f \in \prod\limits_{\zeta < \lambda} \theta_\zeta$, 
            
            \item[(d)]   $\eta \triangleleft f$. 
        \end{enumerate}
            
        \item[$(\beta)$]  $p \le_{\mathbb Q} q$ iff: 
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)]  $\eta^p \trianglelefteq \eta^q$,
            
            
            \item[(b)]  $f^p \le f^q$, i.e. $(\forall \varepsilon < \lambda)
            f^p(\varepsilon) \le f^q(\varepsilon)$, 
            
            \item[(c)]  if $\ell g(\eta^p) \le \varepsilon < \ell g(\eta^q)$ then $\eta^q(\varepsilon) \in [f^p(\varepsilon),\lambda)$, actually follows.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}

    2) The generic is $\let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-

label: z35
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{z35}\ 
    1) We say that a forcing notion
    $\mathbb P$ is $\alpha$-strategically complete \underline{when}  for each $p \in \mathbb P$ in the  following game $\Game_\alpha(p,\mathbb P)$ between the players COM and INC, the player COM has a winning strategy.
    
    A play lasts $\alpha$ moves; in the $\beta$-th move, first the player
    COM chooses $p_\beta \in \mathbb P$ such that $p \le_{\mathbb P} p_\beta$
    and $\gamma < \beta \Rightarrow q_\gamma \le_{\mathbb P} p_\beta$ and
    second the player INC chooses $q_\beta \in \mathbb P$ such that $p_\beta
    \le_{\mathbb P} q_\beta$.
    
    The player COM wins a play if he has a legal move for every $\beta < \alpha$.
    
    2) We say that a forcing notion $\mathbb P$ is $(< \lambda)$-strategically
    complete \underline{when} it is $\alpha$-strategically complete for every
    $\alpha < \lambda$.
    
    Basic properties of ${\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}$ are summarized and proved in
    \cite[\S2]{Sh:949}.

label: c4
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{c4}
    1) Let $\mathbf M$ be the class of objects $\mathbf m$,  called iteration parameters, of the following form (so really $\mathbf M
    = \mathbf M[\bar\lambda]$ and if we omit sub-clauses
    $(\theta), (\iota)$ of clause (e) we may write $\mathbf M[*]$). 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  $L$, a partial order,
        
        \item[(b)]  $M \subseteq L$, as partial orders, (in the main case $M$ is  linearly ordered), 
        
        \item[(c)]  $(\alpha) \quad  u = \langle u_t:t \in L \rangle,$ $\bar{{\mathscr P}} = \langle {\mathscr P}_t:t \in L\rangle,$ each ${\mathscr P}_{t}$ is closed under subsets and ${\mathscr P}_{t} \subseteq [u_{t}]^{\leq \lambda},$
          
        \item[${{}}$]  $(\beta) \quad u_t \subseteq \{s \in L:s <_L t\},$
         
        \item[(d)]   $\rm{dp}(L) < \infty$, that is $L$ is well founded, 
        
        \item[(e)]  
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[$(\alpha)$] $E'$ is a two-place relation (on $L$),
            
            \item[$(\beta)$] $E'' := E' {\restriction} (L \setminus M)$ is an equivalence relation on $L \setminus M,$
            
            \item[$(\gamma)$] the order $\leq_{L}$ is the transitive closure of $\bigcup \{ \leq_{L} {\restriction} (s / E'): s \in L \setminus M \} \cup \{ \leq_{L} {\restriction}  M\},$ equivalently (using $(\delta)$-$(\eta)$ below): 
            
            \begin{itemize}
                \item if $s, t \in L \setminus M$ are not $E''$-equivalent, then $s <_{L}$ t \underline{iff} for some $r_{1} \leq_{{\mathbf m}} r_{2},$ we have $s \leq_{{\mathbf m}} r_{2}$ from $\in s / E_{{\mathbf m}}', r_{2} \leq_{{\mathbf m}} t, r_{2} \in t / E_{{\mathbf m}}',$
                
                \item if $s \in L \setminus M$ and $t \in M,$ then $s \leq_{L} t$ \underline{iff} for some $r \in (s / E') \cap M$ we have $s < r \leq t,$
                
                \item if $s \in M$ and $t \in L \setminus M,$ then $s <_{L} t$ \underline{iff} for some $r \in (t / E') \cap M$ we have $s \leq r < t.$ 
            \end{itemize}
            
            \item[$(\delta)$] if $s E' t$ then $s \notin M \vee t \notin \in M,$
            
            \item[$({\varepsilon})$] is $t \in L \setminus M$ then $\{ s \in L: s E' t \} = \{ s \in L: t E' s \};$ we call it $t / E';$ so $E'$ is a symmetric relation,
            
            \item[$(\zeta)$] if $s, t \in L \setminus M$ are $E''$-equivalent then $s / E' = t / E',$
            
            \item[$(\eta)$] if $t \in  L \setminus M$ then $u_{t} \subseteq t / E',$
            
            \item[$(\theta)$] if $t \in L \setminus M$ then $t / E'$ has cardinality $\leq \lambda_{2},$
            
            \item[$(\iota)$] $\Vert M \Vert \leq \lambda_{1},$
        \end{enumerate}
        
        \item[(f)] disjoint subsets $M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{fat}}, M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{lean}}$ of $M_{{\mathbf m}}$ such that: 
        
        \begin{itemize}
            \item if $s \in M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{fat}}$ then ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, s} = [u_{t}]^{\leq \lambda},$
            
            \item if $s \in M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{lean}}$ then $u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, s} \Rightarrow (\exists t)(u \subseteq t / E_{{\mathbf m}})$
            
            \item we let $M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{non}} = M_{{\mathbf m}} \setminus (M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{fat}} \cup M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{lean}}).$
        \end{itemize}
    \end{enumerate}
    
    2) Saying ${\mathbf m} \in  M$ is lean means that $M_{{\mathbf m}} = M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{lean}}.$ The lean context means that we restrict ourselves to lean ${\mathbf m}$: similarly for fat and neat, see below.
    
    3) We say ${\mathbf m} \in M$ is fat \underline{when} $M_{{\mathbf m}} = M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{fat}}$ and moreover $t \in L_{{\mathbf m}} \Rightarrow {\mathscr P}_{t} = [u_{t}]^{\leq \lambda}.$ 
    
    4) $M_{{\mathbf m}}$ is neat \underline{when} $M_{{\mathbf m}} = M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{lean}} \cup M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{fat}}.$

label: c5d
title: Discussion
body_md:
\label{c5d} 
    Concerning the aim of the choice to use $u_t$ (and ${\mathscr P}_t$) in \ref{c4}, note the following.

    1) By the partial order we already can get partial memory, so why not simply use only $u_t  
    := \{s:s <_L   t\}$?  After all, the index set is only partially ordered, not necessarily linearly, so these sets can be independent of each other.  The reason is that a partial order is transitive, so this simple definition would imply $s \in u_t  \Rightarrow u_s \subseteq u_ t $   which means (by definition)  the memory is transitive,  but  we do not want that to hold in general, (this is central in \cite{Sh:592}).  Here  $\bar u$ is not necessarily transitive, that is,  $s \in u_t \nRightarrow u_s \subseteq u_t$.  By a  partial order we cannot get it.

    2) In \cite{Sh:700}, \cite{Sh:700a}  we use ${\mathscr P}_t$'s which are ideals, but here not
    necessarily: this helps, but has  a price; we are relying on  ``${\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}$ is close to
    being $\lambda$-centered", i.e. any subset of $\{p \in {\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}:{\rm tr}(p) = \eta\}$ of cardinality $< \theta_{\ell g(\eta)}$ has a lub in this forcing. But for the fat context we get more  than $(< \lambda)$-complete ideal.  

    3) What is the point of ``${\mathbf m}$ being neat''? It tells us that in that case it is easy to be an automorphism of ${\mathbf m},$ see \ref{c11}(2), we may forget to say we use it.

label: c10
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{c10}
    1) A reader may wonder, e.g.:
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[$(*)$] if $\langle {\mathbf B}_{\alpha}: \alpha < \alpha_{*} \leq \lambda \rangle$ is a sequence of $\lambda$-Borel  subsets of $\Pi_{{\varepsilon} < \lambda} \theta_{{\varepsilon}}$ which form a partition (in ${\mathbf V}$), does they from a partition also in ${\mathbf V}^{{\mathbb P}}.$ 
    \end{itemize}
    
    In our case as ${\mathbb P}$ is $\lambda$-strategically complete (see \ref{c11}(3A)) the answer is obviously yes. 
    
    2) Note that in $(*)$ we cannot weaken the assumption too much because ``if ${\mathbb P}$ add a new subset to $\theta < \lambda$ this certainly faill''. Even $(< \lambda)$-strategically complete is not enough. Why? assume $\lambda$ is a Mahlo cardinal $S \subseteq \{ \theta < \lambda: \theta$ inaccessible$\}$ is stationary, such that (for transparency) $\diamond_{S}$ holds. We can find ${\mathscr T}$ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\boxplus$ (a)] ${\mathscr T}$ a subtree of $({}^{\lambda}2, \lhd),$
        
        \item[(b)] ${\mathscr T}$ with no $\lhd$-maximal nodes,
        
        \item[(c)] if $\delta \in \lambda \setminus S$ a limit ordinal, $\eta \in {}^{\delta}2$ and $\alpha < \delta \Rightarrow \eta {\restriction} \alpha \in {\mathscr T},$ then $\eta \in {\mathscr T},$
        
        \item[(d)] ${\mathscr T}$ has no $\lambda$-branch. 
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Let ${\mathbf B}_{0} = \{ \eta \in {}^{\lambda}2: \bigwedge_{\alpha < \lambda} \eta {\restriction} \alpha \in {\mathscr T} \}$ and ${\mathbf B}_{1} = {}^{\lambda}2.$
    
    In ${\mathbf V}$ those two $\lambda$-Borel sets form a partition: the first is empty and the second is all.  The forcing notion ${\mathscr T}$ add a $\lambda$-branch to ${\mathscr T},$ hence $({\mathbf B}_{0}, {\mathbf B}_{1})$ are no longer disjoint so fail to form a partition of ${}^{\lambda}2.$ Lastly, for $\alpha < \lambda$ the forcing notion ${\mathscr T}$ is $\alpha$-strategically complete (just COM choose $p_{\alpha} \in {\mathscr T}$ of length $> \alpha$). 
    
    3) Alternatively, if it suffice to us to have ``for $\alpha < \kappa$, COM do not lose in the game of length $\alpha$''  let $\lambda$ be inaccessible and $S$ as above or just such that  $\lambda \setminus S$ is fat i.e. for every club $E$ of $\lambda$ and $\alpha < \lambda$ there is an increasing continuous $h: \alpha \to E$ such that $S \cap {\rm rang}(h) = \emptyset.$ Let ${\mathbb Q} = \{\eta: \eta \in {}^{\lambda >}\lambda$ be increasing continuous with range disjoint to $S$ and $\sup({\rm rang}(\eta_{i}))$ is not in $S\}.$ Let the sequence $\langle \eta_{i}: i < \lambda \rangle$ of pairwise $\unlhd$-incomparable be such that $\lg(\eta_{i}) \in S$ and $(\forall \alpha < \lg(\eta_{i}))[\eta_{i} {\restriction} \alpha \in {\mathbb Q}]$ and it is dense in ${\mathbb Q}.$ For $i < \lambda,$ let ${\mathbf B}_{1 +i}$ be $\{ \nu \in {}^{\lambda} \lambda: \eta_{i} \lhd \nu \},$ so closed and ${\mathbf B}_{0} = \{\nu \in {}^{\lambda}\lambda: \nu$ is not increasing continuous$\},$ now $\langle {\mathbf B}_{i}: i < \lambda \rangle$ is as required.  
    
    4) Another avenue is to assume $\aleph_{0} < \theta = {\rm cf}(\theta) < \lambda, S_{0} \subseteq \{ \delta < \lambda: {\rm cf}(\lambda) < \theta \}, S \subseteq \{ \delta < \lambda: {\rm cf}(\delta) = \theta$ and $S_{0} \cap \delta$ is a stationary subset of $\delta \}.$ Now let ${\mathbb Q} = \{\eta: \eta \in {}^{\lambda >} 2$ and for no $\delta \leq \lg(\eta)$ we have $\delta \in S$ and for some club $E$ of $\delta$ do we have $\alpha \in E \cap S_{0} \Rightarrow \eta(\alpha) = 1 \}.$ Continue as in \ref{c10}(3).
    
    5) Note that if in \ref{z35}(1) we let INC to choose first, then \ref{c10}(a) does not work whereas in \ref{c10}(2), (3) this does no matters.  
    
    6) Anyhow in \ref{c9} this is not necessary; it is enough that being a member of ${\mathbb Q}_{\bar{\theta}}$ is a $\lambda$-Borel set.

body_md:
\label{c26}
    1) We define the two-place relation $\le \, = \, \le_{\mathbf M}$ on $\mathbf M$
    as follows: $\mathbf m \le \mathbf n$ {\underline{iff}}:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  $L_{\mathbf m} \subseteq L_{\mathbf n}$, as partial orders of course,
        
        \item[(b)]  $M_{\mathbf m} = M_{\mathbf n}$, (yes! equal), and $M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{fat}} = M_{{\mathbf n}}^{\rm{fat}}, M_{{\mathbf m}}^{\rm{lean}} = M_{{\mathbf n}}^{\rm{lean}},$ 
        
        \item[(c)]   $u_{\mathbf m,t} = u_{\mathbf n,t} \cap L_{\mathbf m}$ and\footnote{This is the parallel in clause (d) are covered by clause (f) but see part (2).} ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, t} = \{ u \cap L_{{\mathbf m}}: u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, t} \}$ for $t \in M_{\mathbf m}$,
        
        \item[(d)]  $u_{\mathbf m,t} = u_{\mathbf n,t}$ and ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, t} = {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, t}$ for $t \in L_{\mathbf m} \backslash M_{\mathbf m},$
        
        \item[(e)]  if  $t \in L_{\mathbf m } \backslash M_{\mathbf m}$  then $t/E'_{\mathbf m,} = t/E'_{\mathbf n,} $ hence  $E'_{\mathbf m} = E'_{\mathbf n} {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m}.$
        
        \item[(f)] Hence,
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[$\bullet_{1}$] if $t \in L_{{\mathbf m}} \setminus M_{{\mathbf m}}$ then ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, t} = {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, t},$
            
            \item[$\bullet_{2}$]if $t \in M_{{\mathbf m}}$ and $s \in L_{{\mathbf m}} \setminus M_{{\mathbf m}}$ then $\{ u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, t}: u \subseteq s / E_{{\mathbf m}} \} = \{ u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, t}: u \subseteq s / E_{{\mathbf n}} \},$
            
            \item[$\bullet_{3}$] if $t \in M_{{\mathbf m}}$ then $\{ u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, t}: u \subseteq M_{{\mathbf m}} \} = \{ u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, t}: u \subseteq M_{{\mathbf m}} \}$ 
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    
    2) We define the two-place relation $\le_* = \le^*_{\mathbf M}$ as in part (1) omitting clauses (b),(e) and (f); natural but not used 
    here.
     
    3) We define the two-place relation $\leq_{{\mathbf M}}^{\rm{bd}}$ by ${\mathbf m} \leq_{{\mathbf M}}^{\rm{bd}} {\mathbf n}$ iff ${\mathbf m} \leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\mathbf n}$ and both are bounded, see \ref{c5}(10).

    1) $\le_{\mathbf M}$ is a partial order or ${\mathbf M}$ and $\leq_{{\mathbf M}}^{\rm{bd}}$ a partial order on ${\mathbf M}_{\rm{{\rm bd}}}$ in fact is $\leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\restriction} {\mathbf M}_{\rm{bd}}$.

    3) If $\mathbf m \le_{\mathbf M} \mathbf n$ and $L \subseteq L_{\mathbf m}$ {\underline{then}} \, $p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L) \Leftrightarrow p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n}(L)$ for
    every $p$.
    
    4) If ${\mathbf m} \le_{\mathbf{M} } {\mathbf n}$ and ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m} \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n}$ and $L \subseteq L_{\mathbf m}$ {\underline{then}} \, ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L) = {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n}(L)$ 
    as quasi orders.
    
    5) if ${\mathbf m} \leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\mathbf n}$ \underline{then}: 
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ${\mathbf m}$ is lean \underline{iff} ${\mathbf n}$ is lean, 
        
        \item ${\mathbf m}$ is fat \underline{if}\footnote{Why not ``iff''? because maybe ${\mathbf m}$ is fat but for some $t \in L_{{\mathbf n}} \setminus L_{{\mathbf m}}, {\mathscr P}_{t} \neq [u_{t}]^{\leq \lambda}.$} ${\mathbf n}$ is fat, 
        
        \item ${\mathbf m}$ is neat \underline{if} ${\mathbf n}$ is neat,
        
        \item ${\mathbf m}$ is bounded \underline{if} ${\mathbf n}$ is.

asy.  
    
    1) Obvious. 
    
    2) Why is $L_{\mathbf m_\delta} := \cup\{L_{\mathbf m_\alpha}: \alpha <
    \delta\}$ well founded?  Toward contradiction assume $\bar t = \langle t_n:n < \omega\rangle$ is $<_{L_{\mathbf m_\delta}}$-decreasing.  We can
    replace $\bar t$ by any infinite sub-sequence.  So {\rm without loss of generality}: 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)$]  either $(\alpha)$ or $(\beta)$,  where:

        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[$(\alpha)$]  for every $n < m$ there is $s_{n,m} \in M_{\mathbf m_0}$ such that $t_m <_{L_\delta} s_{n,m} <_{L_\delta} t_n,$
            
            \item[$(\beta)$]  for no $n < m$ this holds.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    
    If clause $(\alpha)$ holds, then $\langle s_{n,n+1}:n < \omega\rangle$ is a $<_{M_{{\mathbf m}_0}}$-decreasing sequence contradiction. If clause $(\beta)$ holds, then for $n < \omega$, let $\alpha(n) = \min\{\alpha:t_n \in L_{\mathbf m_\alpha}\}$; {\rm without loss of generality} \, the sequence $ \langle \alpha ( n ) : n < \omega  \rangle $  is monotonically increasing or constant; so as $M_{\mathbf m_{\alpha(n)}} = M_{\mathbf m_0}$,  by \ref{c26}(1)(e) we get $t_n/E_{\mathbf m_{\alpha(n+1)}} =  t_{n+1}/E_{\mathbf m_{\alpha(n+1)}}$  (recalling part (1)),   hence $t_{n+1} \in  L_{\mathbf m_{\alpha(n)}}$ hence $\alpha(n+1) \le \alpha(n)$.
    So $\{t_n:n < \omega\} \subseteq M_{{\mathbf m}_{\alpha(0)}}$ hence as 
    $L_{\mathbf m_{\alpha(n)}}$ is well founded we are done.
    
    The proofs of (2A) and (2B) are easy too. 
     
    Finally for (3), (4) and (5), see the proof of $\boxplus_\alpha$ in the proof of \ref{c33s}.

body_md:
\label{c32n}
    1) For $ p,q \in \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} $ we have:  $ \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} \models {\text{`}\text{`}} p \le q" $  \underline{iff} $ {\rm dom} (p) \subseteq   {\rm dom}(q)$  and  $ q $ is essentially above $ p $ inside  $ \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} $, (see \ref{c5}(9) or below).  
        
    2) For $p,q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}$ the following conditions are equivalent:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  $q \Vdash ``p \in \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\mathbf G$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}}"$,  that is $ q $ is essentially above $ p$, see \ref{c5}(9), 
        
        \item[(b)]  if $s \in {\rm dom}(p)$ {\underline{then}} \, either $s \in {\rm dom}(q)$ and $(q {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,< s}) \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m,<s}} ``p(s) \le q(s)"$ \underline{or} $s \notin {\rm dom}(q),{\rm tr}(p(s)) = \emptyset$ and $q
        {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m,<s}} ``p(s)$ is trivial,  i.e. $\let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3f$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{p(s)}$ is constantly zero",
        
        \item[(c)]  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m} \models ``p \le q^+"$ where ${\rm dom}(q^+) = {\rm dom}(q) \cup {\rm dom}(p)$ and $q^+(s)$ is: 
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[$(\alpha)$]  $q(s)$ if $s \in {\rm dom}(q)$, 
            
            \item[$(\beta)$]  the trivial condition if $s \in {\rm dom}(p) \backslash {\rm dom}(q)$; note that ${\rm fsupp}(q^+) = {\rm fsupp}(q) \cup
            {\rm fsupp}(p)$.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
) Easy but we shall elaborate.
     
    Let $ p, q \in \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} $. 
    If $ p \le q $ then clearly ${\rm dom}(p) \subseteq {\rm dom}(q)$  and $ q \Vdash _{\mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m}} {\text{`}\text{`}} p \in \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3 \mathbf{G} $\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}"$, that is  $ q $  is essentially above $p$. 
    
    For the other direction assume 
    ${\rm dom}(p) \subseteq {\rm dom}(q)$ but $ \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} \models \neg ( p \le q )$ and we shall prove that $ q $ is not essentially  above $p,$ this suffices.  By the present assumption there is $ s \in {\rm dom}(p) $ (hence $ s \in {\rm dom}(q)$) but $ q {\restriction} L_{ {\mathbf m} (< s)} \not\Vdash  {\text{`}\text{`}} p(s) \le q(s)"$. 
    
    Hence there is $q_{1} \in {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m} (< s)}$ above $q {\restriction} L_{{\mathbf m}(<s)}$ such that $q_{1} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}}(< s)}$``$\neg (p(s) \leq q(s))$''. By the properties of ${\mathbb Q}_{\bar{\theta}}$ (and ${\mathbb Q}_{s}'$, \ref{c11}(6)) there are $q_{2}, q'$ such that: 
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[$(*)_{1}$]
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)] $q' \in {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}}, {\rm dom}(q') = \{ s\},$
            
            \item[(b)] $q_{1} \leq q_{2}$ in ${\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m} (< s)},$
            
            \item[(c)] $q_{2} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}{{\mathbf m}(s)}}$``$q(s) \leq q'(s)$ but $q'(s), p(s)$ are incompatible''
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{itemize}
    
    Lastly, choose the function $q_{3}$ by: 
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[$(*)_{2}$] 
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)] ${\rm dom}(q_{3}) = {\rm dom}(q_{2}) \cup {\rm dom}(q),$
            
            \item[(b)] $q_{3} {\restriction} {\rm dom}(q_{2}) = q_{2},$
            
            \item[(c)] $q_{3}(s) = q'(s),$
            
            \item[(d)] $q_{2}(t) = q(t)$ if $t \in {\rm dom}(p) \setminus ({\rm dom}(q_{2}) \cup \{ s \}). $
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{itemize}
    
    Clearly $q_{3} \in {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}}, q \leq q_{3}$ and $q_{3} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}}}$``$p \notin \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3{\mathbb Q}$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{{\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}}}$'' so we are done. 
    
    2) \underline{(a) implies (c)}:
    
    By the choice of $ q^+ $ we have $ q \le q^+$, so clause (a) implies  that $ q $ is essentially above $ p $ hence by part (1) in $ \mathbb{P} _\mathbf{m} $ we have $ p \le q^+ $ so clearly
    clause (c) holds.
     
    \underline{(c) implies (a)}:
     
    Easy.
    
    \underline{(c) iff (b)}:
    
    Obvious recalling the properties of ${\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}$.

body_md:
\label{c35p}
    1) We may phrase it differently.  Recall that assuming ${\mathbb P}' \lessdot {\mathbb P}$, we say $p' \in {\mathbb P}'$ is a reduction of $p \in {\mathbb P}$ where every condition $r \in {\mathbb P}'$ stronger     than $p'$ (in $ \mathbb{P} ' $)  is still compatible (in ${\mathbb P}$) with $p$.   Let $ \mathbb{P} _ {\ell} = \mathbb{P}_\mathbf{m}   (L_ {\ell} )$.  
    Now the statement is: to find a reduction of $p_3$ from  $ \mathbb{P} _3 $ to $ \mathbb{P} _ 1 $  first consider $p_2 =$ the reduction of $ p_3 $ to $\mathbb{P} _ 2 $,    then let $p_0$ be a reduction of $p_2$ from  $ \mathbb{P} _2 $ to $ \mathbb{P}_{0}$ and finally extend $p_0$ to a condition $p_1$ by appending the information from $p_3$ on ($L_{1}$ minus $L_{0}$).
     
    2) Claim \ref{c33n} is used only in the
    proof of \ref{c33s} which is used only in the
    proof of \ref{e35} and \ref{e37}.

title: Proof
body_md:
s ${\rm dp}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) < \infty$ it suffices to  prove by induction on the ordinal $\gamma$ that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\boxplus_\gamma$]  if $\langle L_\ell:\ell \le 3\rangle$ satisfies $(*)$ of the claim and ${\rm dp}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \le \gamma$ {\underline{then}}:
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[$\bullet_1$]  we have $p_1 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$ and $p_1 \le q_1 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \Rightarrow p_3,q_1$ are compatible in
            ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$ {\underline{when}}:
            
             
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item[$(a) $]  $p_3 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3),$
                
                \item[$(b) $]  $p_0 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0),$
                
                \item[$(c) $]   if $p_0 \le q_0 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0)$ 
                {\underline{then}} \, $p_2 := p_3 {\restriction} L_2$ and $q_0$ are compatible in
                $P_{\mathbf m}(L_2),$
                
                \item[$(d) $] $p_1 = p_0 \cup (p_3 {\restriction} (L_1 \backslash L_0))$.
            \end{enumerate}
            
            \item[$\bullet_2$]  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3).$
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}

    Why this holds?  Assume we have arrived to $\gamma$.
    
    \underline{Clause $\bullet_1$}:  (notice that here we do not  use the induction hypothesis): 
    Recalling clause (f) of the assumption,
    indeed, $p_1 = p_0 \cup (p_3 {\restriction} (L_1 \backslash L_0))  \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$ by the definitions (clauses $\bullet_1 (a)), (b), (d) $  of $\boxplus_\gamma$), e.g. why
    ${\rm fsupp}(p_1) \subseteq L_1$?  Note that if $s \in {\rm dom}(p_3 {\restriction} (L_1 \backslash L_0)$ then $s \in L_1 \backslash L_0 \subseteq L_1$ and
    $\{r_{p_3(s)}(\zeta):\zeta < \xi_{p(s)}\}$ is included in $L_3$ because $p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$ and in $L_{<s}$ by Definition
    \ref{c6}.  As $s \in L_1 \backslash L_0$ by $(*)(e)$ we have $s \notin M_{\mathbf m}$ hence by Definition \ref{c6} we have $\{r_{p_3(s)}(\zeta):\zeta < \xi_{p(s)}\} \subseteq u_s \subseteq s/E_{\mathbf m}$.  By $(*)(f)$ we have $(s/E_{\mathbf m})
    \cap L_{\mathbf m <t} \subseteq L_1$ hence together $\{r_{p_3(s)}(\zeta):\zeta < \xi_{p(s)}\} \subseteq L_1$, and we are done proving ${\rm fsupp}(p_1) \subseteq L_1$.
    
    So the first statement in $\boxplus_\gamma \bullet_{1}$ holds; what about the second?  Toward contradiction assume $q_1$ contradicts the
    desired conclusion. Then by \ref{c11}(6) there are $s$ and $p^+_3$ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\oplus$]  $(a) \quad s \in {\rm dom}(q_1) \cap {\rm dom}(p_3)$,
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(b) \quad p^+_3 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_{\mathbf m,<s})$, 
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(c) \quad p^+_3$ is above $p_3 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s}$ and above $q_1 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s}$,  
          
        \item[${{}}$]  $(d) \quad p^+_3 \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m,<s}} ``p_3(s),q_1(s) \in {\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}$ are incompatible (in
        ${\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}$)".
    \end{enumerate}
    
    So $s \in {\rm dom}(q_1) \subseteq L_1$ and as $L_2$ is an initial segment of $L_{\mathbf m}$ and
    clause  (c) of  $ \bullet _2 $ 
    (of $\boxplus_\gamma$),  clearly $s \in L_0$ is impossible, so $s \in {\rm dom}(q_1) \backslash L_0
    \subseteq L_1 \backslash L_0$. As ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m} \models ``p_1 \le q_1"$, necessarily $q_1 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m,<s}} ``p_1(s) \le q_1(s)"$, so as
    $q_1 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \le p^+_3 {\restriction} 
    L_{\mathbf m,<s}$ (by $\oplus(c))$, 
    also $p^+_3 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m,<s}} 
    ``p_1(s) \le q_1(s)"$.  As $s \notin L_0$ clearly $p_1(s) = p_3(s)$ by clauses $\boxplus_\gamma  \bullet _2 (b), (d) $, so  $p^+_3 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m,<s}} 
    ``p_3(s) \le q_1(s)"$ and again easy contradiction to $\oplus(d)$.
    
    \underline{Clause $\bullet_2$}:  
    
    Clearly ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \subseteq {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$ as quasi orders.  Next we shall prove ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \le_{{\rm ic}}
    {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$, so assume $q_1,q_2 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$ has a common upper bound $p_3$ in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$, and we should find one in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$.  Hence (see \ref{c6}(e)$(\beta)$) we have  ${\rm dom}(q_1) \cup {\rm dom}(q_2) \subseteq {\rm dom}(p_3)$.
    
    As $p_3 {\restriction} L_2 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)$ by $(*)(a)$ and  we are assuming ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)$,
    see $(*)(d)$ there is $p_0 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0)$ such that $p_0 \le q \in
    {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0) \Rightarrow q,p_3 {\restriction} L_2$ are compatible in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)$ and let $p_1 = p_0 \cup (p_3 {\restriction} (L_1 \backslash L_0))$.  By  $\boxplus_\gamma(b)$, which we have proved noting that clauses (a)-(d) of $\boxplus_\gamma   \bullet _2 $  holds, we know that  $p_1 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$ and $p_1 \le p'_1 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \Rightarrow p_3,p'_1$ are compatible in
    ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$. It suffices to prove that $p_1$ is a common upper
    bound of $q_1,q_2$.
    
    We could have replaced $p_0$ by $p'_0$ whenever $p_0 \le p'_0 \in  {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0)$.  So {\rm without loss of generality} \, for $\ell=1,2$ we have  ${\rm dom}(q_\ell) \cap L_0 \subseteq {\rm dom}(p_0)$ hence $\subseteq {\rm dom}(p_1)$, also recall ${\rm dom}(q_\ell) \backslash L_0 \subseteq {\rm dom}(p_3) \cap L_1 \backslash L_0$ and by the choice of $p_1$ we have ${\rm dom}(p_3) \cap L_1 \backslash L_0 \subseteq {\rm dom}(p_1) \backslash L_0$.
    
    So recalling ${\rm dom}(q_\ell) \subseteq L_1$
    together ${\rm dom}(q_\ell) \subseteq {\rm dom}(p_1)$.
    
    As we are assuming ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)$ 
    {\rm without loss of generality} \,  $p_0$ is above\footnote{Why?  It suffices to prove that there is $p'_0 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0)$ above $p_0$ and above $q_\ell {\restriction} L_0$. So toward contradiction assume this fails hence there  is $p^+_0 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0)$  above $p_0$ incompatible with $q_\ell {\restriction} L_0$.  By the choice 
    of $p_0$ we know that $p^+_0,(p_3 {\restriction} L_2)$ are compatible, so  let $p^+_3 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)$ be a common upper bound.   Now $L_2$ is an initial segment of $L_{\mathbf m}$ by $(*)(a)$ and $p_3$ is above $q_\ell$ hence $p_3 {\restriction} L_2$ is above $q_\ell {\restriction} L_2$
    and as $q_\ell \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1),L_0 = L_1 \cap L_2$ we have $q_\ell {\restriction} L_2 = q_\ell {\restriction} L_0,p_3 {\restriction} L_2$ is above $q_\ell
    {\restriction} L_0$ but $p^+_3$ is above $p_3 {\restriction} L_2$ hence  $p^+_3$ is above $q_\ell {\restriction} L_2$. 
    Also $p^+_3$ is above $p^+_0$ which forces $q_\ell {\restriction} L_0 \notin \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\mathbf G$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_0)}$, equivalently
    $q_\ell {\restriction} L_0 \notin \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\mathbf G$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)}$, contradiction.} 
    $q_\ell {\restriction} L_0$.  If toward contradiction we assume that $\ell \in \{1,2\}$ and $q_\ell \nleq p_1$ then for some $s \in {\rm dom}(q_\ell)$ we have $(q_\ell {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s}) \le (p_1 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s})$ but $p_1 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \nVdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_{\mathbf m,<s})} ``q_\ell(s) \le  p_1(s)"$.  Clearly, $s \in L_0$ is impossible so $s \in L_1 \backslash L_0$ hence $s \notin M_{\mathbf m}$ by clause $(*)(e)$.
     
    Let $L'_0 = L_0,L'_1 = L_0 \cup (L_1 \cap L_{\mathbf m,<s}),L'_2 = L_2,L'_3 = L_3$ so $(L'_0,L'_1,L'_2,L'_3)$ satisfies the assumptions
    of the present claim and ${\rm dp}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1) < \gamma$,  hence by the induction hypothesis, ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_3)$.
    
    Recall $s \in L_1 \backslash L_0$ hence $(s/E_{\mathbf m}) \cap L_{\mathbf m,<s}
    \subseteq L_1$ by clause (f) of the assumption of the claim, so ${\rm fsupp}(p_1 {\restriction} \{s\}) \backslash \{s\},{\rm fsupp}(q_\ell {\restriction} \{s\}) \backslash \{s\}$ are $\subseteq L'_1$ hence $p_1(s),q_\ell(s)$ are ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1)$-names.  So recalling $p_1 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s} \nVdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_{\mathbf m,<s})} ``q_\ell(s) \le p_1(s)"$ and ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1) \lessdot
    {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_3)$ and $L_{\mathbf m,<s} \subseteq L_3 = L'_3$ we  have $p_1 {\restriction} L'_1 \nVdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1)} ``q_\ell(s) \le
    p_1(s)"$. Hence there is $p^+_1$ such that $p_1 {\restriction} L'_1 \le p^+_1 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1)$ such that $p^+_1  \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1)} ``q_\ell(s) \nleq p_1(s)"$ so recalling
    ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1) \lessdot {\mathbb P}(L'_3)$ we have $p^+_1 \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_3)} ``q_\ell(s) \nleq p_1(s)"$.
    
    But by $\boxplus_{\gamma_1}  \bullet _2$ 
    for $\gamma_1 = {\rm dp}_{\mathbf m}(L'_1)$, we
    know that $p^+_1$ and $p_3 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s}$  are compatible (in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}$,
    equivalently ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_{\mathbf m,<s}))$ so let $p^+_3 \in {\mathbb P}_\mathbf{m}  (L_{\mathbf m,<s})$ be a common upper bound of $p^+_1,p_3 {\restriction} L_{\mathbf m,<s}$.  Now $p^+_3 \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_3)} ``q_\ell(s)
    \le p_1(s)"$ because: $q_\ell \le p_3$ by the choice of $p_3$; $p_1(s) = p_3(s)$ by the choice of $p_1$ and $p_3 \le p^+_3$, see above.
    However, $p^+_3 \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L'_3)}  ``q_\ell(s) \nleq p_1(s)"$ as $p^+_1
    \le p^+_3$, see above.
    
    So we have proved ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \le_{{\rm ic}} {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$.
    
    To finish proving clause $\boxplus_\gamma  \bullet_{1},$  that is, ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$ note that clause $\boxplus_\gamma  \bullet_{1}$  does this as for every $p_3 \in  {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_3)$ there is $p_0$ as in $\boxplus_\gamma  \bullet _1 (b), (c)$  by clause (d) of the claim's assumption and let $p_1$ be as defined in $\boxplus_\gamma   \bullet_{1} (d)$.

body_md:
or $\ell \in \{1,2\}$ let $\bar L_\ell = \langle L_{\ell,i}:i < 4 \rangle$ be defined by:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\oplus_1$]  $(a) \quad L_{\ell,0} = L_0$,
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(b) \quad L_{\ell,1} = L_1$, 
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(c) \quad L_{\ell,2} = \{s \in L_{\mathbf m_\ell}:s \le_{\mathbf m_\ell} t$ for some $t \in L_0\}$,
    
        \item[${{}}$]  $(d) \quad L_{\ell,3} = L_{\mathbf m_\ell}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Clearly,
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\oplus_2$]  $(a) \quad (\mathbf m_\ell,\bar L_\ell)$ satisfies the assumptions of \ref{c33n} hence,
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(b) \quad {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_{\ell,1}) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_{\ell,3})$ which means ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_1) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}$ for $\ell=1,2$.
    \end{enumerate}

    Why $\oplus_2$? Clearly it suffices to prove clause (a), so we just have to check clauses  $(*)(a)-(f)$ of \ref{c33n}.
    
    \underline{Clause $(*)(a)$}:
    
    By $\oplus_1(d),L_{\ell,3} = L_{\mathbf m_\ell}$ hence is an initial segment of $L_{\mathbf m_\ell}$ and by $\oplus_1(c),L_{\ell,2}$  is an initial segment of $L_{\mathbf m_\ell}$ which is $L_{\ell,3}$ so $L_{\ell,2} \subseteq L_{\ell,3}$.
    
    \underline{Clause $(*)(b)$}:
    
    For the first statement, $L_{\ell,1} \subseteq L_{\ell,3}$ is trivial by $\oplus_1(d) + \oplus_1(b) + \boxdot(a),(b)$.   The second statement says $L_{\ell,0} = L_{\ell,1}
    \cap L_{\ell,2}$.  Now $L_{\ell,0} \subseteq L_{\ell,1}$ by $\boxdot(a),(b)$ of the claim and $\oplus_1(a),(b)$.  Also $L_{\ell,0}
    \subseteq L_{\ell,2}$ holds by $\oplus_1(c)$ (and $\oplus_1(a)$). Together $L_{\ell,0} \subseteq L_{\ell,1} \cap L_{\ell,2}$; to prove
    the inverse inclusion assume $s \in L_{\ell,2} \cap L_{\ell,1}$, so as $s \in L_{\ell,2}$ by $\oplus_1(c)$ there is $t \in L_0$ such that $s
    \le_{\mathbf m_\ell} t$.  But $s \in L_{\ell,1} = L_1$ so by $\boxdot(c)$ of the claim we have $s \in L_0 = L_{\ell,0}$ as promised.
    
    \underline{Clause $(*)(c)$}:
    
    Holds by  condition $\boxdot(c)$ of the claim.
    
    \underline{Clause $(*)(d)$}:
    
    By clause $\boxdot(f)$ of the claim and $\oplus_1(c),L_{\ell,2}$ is an initial segment of $L_{\mathbf m_\ell}$, hence by \ref{c8}(e) we have ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_{\ell,2}) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell} = {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_{\ell,3})$.  By $\boxdot(e) \, 
    {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_0}(L_{\ell,0}) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}$; so together as
    $L_{\ell,0} \subseteq L_{\ell,2}$, we have ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_0) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L_{\ell,2})$. 
    
    \underline{Clauses $(*)(e),(f)$}:
    
    Hold by condition $\boxdot(f)$ of the claim.  
         
    So $\oplus_2$ holds indeed.  So now we deal with the other half.
     
    \underline{Proof of}: ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L_1) = {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L_1)$.
     
    Let $\langle s_\alpha:\alpha < \alpha(*)\rangle$ list $L_1 \backslash L_0$ such that $s_\alpha \le_{L_{\mathbf m}} s_\beta \Rightarrow \alpha
    \le \beta$.  This is possible as $L_{\mathbf m_2}$ is well founded.
     
    Now, 
     
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\oplus_3$]  for $\ell=1,2$ and $\alpha \le \alpha(*)$ let $\bar L^*_{\ell,\alpha} = \langle L^*_{\ell,\alpha,i}:i < 4\rangle$ be (but we can omit $\ell$) where:
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)]  $L^*_{\ell,\alpha,0} = L_0,$
            
            \item[(b)]  $L^*_{\ell,\alpha,1} = L_0 \cup \{s_\beta:\beta < \alpha\},$
            
            \item[(c)]  $L^*_{\ell,\alpha,2} = \{s \in L_{\mathbf m_\ell}:s \le_{\mathbf m_\ell} t$ for some $t \in L_0\},$
            
            \item[(d)]  $L^*_{\ell,\alpha,3} = L_{\mathbf m_\ell},$
        \end{enumerate}
        
        \item[$\oplus_4$]
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item[(a)]  $(\bar{\mathbf m}_\ell,\bar L^*_{\ell,\alpha})$ satisfies the assumption of \ref{c33n},
                
                \item[(b)]  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L^*_{\ell,\alpha,1}) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_\ell}(L^*_{\ell,\alpha,3})$.
            \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    
    [Why?  Note the $\mathbf m_\ell,\langle L^*_{\ell,\alpha,i}:i < 4\rangle$ satisfies the assumptions of \ref{c33n}, hence $\oplus_2$
    holds for $\mathbf m_\ell,\bar L_{\ell,\alpha}$ for $\alpha  \le \alpha(*)$.]
    
    Now by induction on $\alpha \le \alpha(*)$ we prove that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\boxplus_\alpha$]   ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) =  {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\alpha,1})$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    \underline{Case 1}:  $\alpha = 0$:
    
    As $L^*_{1,\alpha,1} = L_0 = L^*_{2,\alpha,1}$, clause $\boxdot(d)$  of the assumption gives $\boxplus_\alpha$ as promised.
    
    \underline{Case 2}:  $\alpha$ a limit ordinal:
    
    Easy by the definition of the iteration.  That is, first,  if $ {\rm dom}(p) \in [L_{\mathbf{m} _2}]^{\le \lambda } $  then  we know $p
    \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \Leftrightarrow \bigwedge\limits_{\beta < \alpha}
    [p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1})] \Leftrightarrow \bigwedge\limits_{\beta < \alpha}
    [p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\beta,1})] \Leftrightarrow p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\alpha,1})$; 
    second, for $p,q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1})$  by the definition of the order and the induction hypothesis, ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$ {\underline{iff}} \, $\bigwedge\limits_{\beta < \alpha} [{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1}) \models ``p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \le q
    {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}"]$ {\underline{iff}} \, $\bigwedge\limits_{\beta < \alpha}
    [{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\beta,1}) \models ``p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \le q
    {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}"]$ {\underline{iff}} \,
    ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$.
    
    So $\boxplus_\alpha$ holds.
    
    \underline{Case 3}:  $\alpha = \beta +1$:
    
    Clearly,

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_1$]  $p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \Leftrightarrow 
        p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\alpha,1})$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Next,
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_2$]  assume $p,q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1})$ and we shall prove that ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$ implies ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    [Why? If $s_\beta \notin {\rm dom}(p)$ this is obvious by the induction hypothesis.  Hence we can assume $s_\beta \in {\rm dom}(p)$, so as we are assuming ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$, clearly $s_\beta \in {\rm dom}(q)$ hence $s_\beta \in {\rm dom}(p) \cap {\rm dom}(q)$.  First, similarly ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1}) \models ``(p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}) \le (q {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1})"$ and $(q {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}) {\Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}_{1} (<s_{\beta})}}} ``p(s_\beta) \le_{{\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}} q(s_\beta)"$ by the definition of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1})$.   Second, as $q {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1}) =  {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\beta,1})$ and ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1}) \lessdot
    {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1  }$  by $\oplus_4$ and ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\beta,1})
    \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}$ by $\oplus_4 $ 
    and $p(s_\beta), q(s_\beta)$ are  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1})$-names  (as ${\rm fsupp}(p(s_\beta),{\rm fsupp}(q(s_\beta))
    \subseteq L^*_{\beta,1})$ necessarily we have $q {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}  \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}} ``p(s_\beta) \le_{{\mathbb Q}_{\bar\theta}} 
    q(s_\beta)"$.  Third, as ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\beta,1})  \models ``p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \le q {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}"$, 
    by the induction hypothesis ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}
    (L^*_{\beta,1}) \models ``p {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1} \le q {\restriction} L^*_{\beta,1}$.  Fourth, by the last two sentence and the definition of
    the order in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}$ we have ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2} \models ``p \le
    q"$ so the conclusion of $(*)_2$ holds also in this case.
    
    Note that if  $s_\beta \in {\rm dom}(p) \backslash {\rm dom}(q)$ then $p \nleq q$, so we are done
    proving $(*)_2$.]
     
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_3$]  if $p,q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}   (L^*_{\alpha,1})$ and ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$ then ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L^*_{\alpha,1}) \models ``p \le q"$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    [Why?  Similar to the proof of $(*)_2$.]
    
    By $(*)_1,(*)_2,(*)_3$ clearly $\boxplus_\alpha$ holds.  So we carried the induction so $\boxplus_\alpha$ holds for every $\alpha \le \alpha(*)$ and for $\alpha = \alpha(*)$ we get ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_1}(L_1) = {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m_2}(L_2)$.  Together with $\oplus_2(b)$ in the beginning of the proof we are done.

et $x = u$ for part (1) and $x = b$ for part (2). Let $\mathscr{X} = \mathscr{X}_{{\mathbf m}} = \{{\mathbf n}: {\mathbf n}$ is bounded if $x = b;$ and $({\mathbf m} {\restriction} M_{{\mathbf m}}) \leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\mathbf n}$ and $L_{{\mathbf n}} \setminus M_{{\mathbf m}} = t / E_{{\mathbf n}}''$ for some $t,$ hence $\Vert L_{{\mathbf n}} \Vert \leq \lambda_{2}\}.$

    We define a two-place relation ${\mathscr E}$ on ${\mathscr X}$:

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_0$]  $\mathbf n_1 {\mathscr E} \mathbf n_2$ {\underline{iff}} \, $(\mathbf n_1,\mathbf n_2 \in {\mathscr X}$ and) there is an isomorphism $h$ from $\mathbf n_1$ onto $\mathbf n_2$ over $\mathbf m {\restriction} M_{\mathbf m}$, 
        that is: an isomorphism from $L_{\mathbf n_1}$  onto $L_{\mathbf n_2}$ over $M_{\mathbf m}$ (as partial orders) such that: 
        
        \begin{enumerate} 
            \item[(a)] $t \in L_{\mathbf n_1} \Rightarrow u_{\mathbf n_2,h(t)} = \{h(s):s  \in u_{\mathbf n_1,t}\}$, 
            
            \item[(b)] $t \in L_{\mathbf n_1} \Rightarrow {\mathscr P}_{\mathbf n_2,h(t)} = \{\{h(s):s \in u\}:u \in {\mathscr P}_{\mathbf n_1,t}\}$, 
            
            \item[(c)] $s,t \in L_{\mathbf n_1} \Rightarrow (s E'_{\mathbf n_1 } t \Leftrightarrow h(s) E'_{\mathbf n_2 } h(t))$.   
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate} 

    Clearly ${\mathscr E}$ is an equivalence relation.
    
    By our assumptions $\chi \ge 2^{\lambda_2}$ and $\mathbf n \in {\mathscr X} \Rightarrow |L_{\mathbf n}| \le \lambda_2 \wedge (\forall t \in L_{{\mathbf n}})({\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, t} \subseteq [L_{{\mathbf n}, < t}]^{\leq \lambda}),$  hence recalling $\lambda_2 = (\lambda_2)^\lambda$  clearly ${\mathscr E}$ has $\le 2^{\lambda_2}$ equivalence classes and let $\langle \mathbf n_\alpha:\alpha <
    2^{\lambda_2} \rangle$ be a set of representatives (not necessary, but no harm
    in allowing repetitions).  
    
    By \ref{c28}(2) and \ref{c31} we can find $\mathbf n$ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_1$]  $(a) \quad \mathbf m \le_{\mathbf M} \mathbf n \in \mathbf M_\chi,$
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(b) \quad$ for every $\alpha < 2^{\lambda_2}$ we can find $\langle t_{\alpha,i}:i < \chi\rangle$ such that:
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[${{}}$]  $(\alpha) \quad t_{\alpha,i} \in L_{\mathbf n} \backslash L_{\mathbf m},$
            
            \item[${{}}$]  $(\beta) \quad (\alpha \ne \beta) \vee (i \ne j)  \Rightarrow t_{\alpha,i}/E_{\mathbf n} \ne t_{\beta,j}/E_{\mathbf n},$
            
            \item[${{}}$]  $(\gamma) \quad \mathbf n {\restriction}  (t_{\alpha,i}/E_{\mathbf n})$ is ${\mathscr E}$-equivalent to $\mathbf n_\alpha$,
            see \ref{c5}(0) on $t_{\alpha,i}/E_{\mathbf n}$.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}

    We shall now  prove that $\mathbf n$ is as required. Let $\mathbf n \le_{\mathbf M} \mathbf n_1 \le_{\mathbf M} \mathbf n_2, $ and $ {\mathbf n}_{1}, {\mathbf n}_{2}$ are bounded when $x = b$   and define ${\mathscr F}$ as the set of functions $f$ such that some $L_1, L_2$ satisfy:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_2$]  $(a) \quad L_\ell \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_\ell}$,
        
        \item[${{}}$]    $(b) \quad M_ \mathbf{m} = M_ \mathbf{n} \subseteq L_1  \cap L_2$,
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(c) \quad L_\ell$ has cardinality $\le \lambda_2$,
        
        \item[${{}}$]  $(d) \quad L_\ell$ is $E_{\mathbf n_{\ell} }$-closed, i.e.  $M_ \mathbf{m} \subseteq L_{\ell}$ and $ t
        \in L_\ell \backslash M_{\mathbf m} \Rightarrow t/E_{\mathbf n_2} \subseteq L_\ell$, 
          
        \item[${{}}$]  $(e) \quad f$ is an isomorphism from  $\mathbf n_2 {\restriction} L_1$ onto $\mathbf n_2 {\restriction} L_2$  over $M_{\mathbf m}$, i.e.:  
        
        \begin{enumerate}
        \item[${{\bullet_1}}$]  $ \quad f$ is a one-to-one mapping from $L_1$ onto $L_2$, 
        
        \item[${{\bullet _2}}$]  $\quad f {\restriction} M_{\mathbf m}$ is the identity,
        
        \item[${{\bullet _3}}$]  $ \quad f$ maps $\le_{\mathbf n_2} {\restriction} L_1$ onto $\le_{\mathbf n_2} {\restriction} L_2$, 
        
        \item[${{\bullet _4}}$] $\quad $  $ s E'_{\mathbf{n} _1}  t  \Leftrightarrow f(s) E'_{\mathbf n_2} f(t)$,
        
        
        \item[${{\bullet _5}}$] $\quad$ for $s,t \in L_1$ we have $s \in u_{\mathbf n_2,t} \Leftrightarrow f(s) \in u_{\mathbf n_2,f(t)}.$
          
        \item[$\bullet_{6}$] for $t \in L_{1}$ we have ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}_{2}, f(t)} = \{ \{ f(s): s \in u \}: u \in {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}_{1}, t}, u \subseteq L_{1} \}.$ 
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Clearly,
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_3$]  if $f \in {\mathscr F}$ and $L' \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_1}, L'' \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_2}$ and $|L'| + |L''| \le \lambda_2$ {\underline{then}} \, for some $g \in {\mathscr F}$ extending $f$ we have: 
        
        \begin{enumerate} 
            \item[(a)] $L' \subseteq {\rm dom}(g) $,
            
            \item[(b)] $ L'' \subseteq {\rm rang}(g)$,  
            
            \item[(c)] ${\rm rang}(g) \backslash (L'' \cup  {\rm rang}(f)) \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_{2}}$,
            
            \item[(d)] ${\rm dom}(g) \backslash (L'   
            \cup  {\rm dom}(f)) \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_{1}}.$
        \end{enumerate} 
    \end{enumerate}
    
    We can finish as in the parallel of the Tarski-Vaught criterion for ${\mathbb L}_{\infty,\lambda^+_2}$  but we shall elaborate.  That is, first we can prove by
    induction on the ordinal $\gamma < |L_{\mathbf n_2}|^+$ (and in fact just $\gamma < \|M_{\mathbf n_2}\|^+$) that $ (*)_4-(*)_6 $ below holds: 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_4$]  letting $L_\gamma = L^{{\rm dp}}_{\mathbf n_2,\gamma}$, if 
        $g \in {\mathscr F}$ {\underline{then}}: 
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)] $g$ maps ${\rm dom}(g) \cap L_\gamma$ onto ${\rm rang}(g) \cap L_\gamma$, 
            
            \item[(b)]  $g$ induces an isomorphism $\hat g$ from  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}({\rm dom}(g) \cap L_\gamma)$ onto ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}({\rm rang}(g) \cap L_\gamma)$, that is: $\hat
            g(p)=q$ \underline{iff}:
            
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item[$(\alpha)$]  $p \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}({\rm dom}(g) \cap L_\gamma)$, 
                
                \item[$(\beta)$]  $q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}({\rm rang}(g) \cap L_\gamma)$, 
                
                \item[$(\gamma)$]  $g$ maps ${\rm dom}(p)$ onto ${\rm dom}(q)$ and $s \in {\rm dom}(p) \Rightarrow {\rm tr}(p(s)) = {\rm tr}(q(g(s)))$, 
                
                \item[$(\delta)$]   if $s \in {\rm dom}(g),g(s) = t \in {\rm rang}(g)$ and $\let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3f$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{p(s)} = \mathbf B_{p(s)}(\ldots, \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\eta$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{r_{p(s)}(\zeta)},\ldots)_{\zeta < \xi_{p(s)}}$ and $f_{q(t)} = \mathbf B_{q(t)}(\ldots,\let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\eta$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{r_{q(t)}(\zeta)},\ldots)_{\zeta < \xi_{q(t)}}$ {\underline{then}} \, $\xi_{q(t)} = \xi_{p(s)},\mathbf B_{q(t)} = \mathbf
                B_{p(s)}$ and $\zeta < \xi_{p(s)} \Rightarrow r_{q(t)}(\zeta) = g(r_{p(s)}(\zeta))$, 
                
                \item[$(\varepsilon)$]   moreover in $(\delta)$ we have $\iota(s,p) = \iota(t,q)$ and if $\iota < \iota(s,p)$ then $w_{p,s,\iota} = w_{q,t,\iota},\mathbf B_{p(s),\iota} = \mathbf B_{q(t),\iota}.$
            \end{enumerate}
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    
    [Why? We use freely \ref{c11}(9). Let $ \chi_* $ be such that $\gamma,  g, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{n}_1,\mathbf{n} _2  \in {\mathscr H} (\chi _*)$.  Let $ \mathfrak{A} \prec ({\mathscr H} (\chi_*), \in ) $ be such that  $\gamma, g, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{n}  _1,\mathbf{n} _2  \in \mathfrak{A} , \| \mathfrak{A} \| = \chi , \chi + 1  \subseteq  \mathfrak{A} $  and $ [\mathfrak{A} ]^{\le \lambda }\subseteq \mathfrak{A} $, (hence $ \mathfrak{A} \prec _{\mathbb{L} _{\lambda ^+, \lambda ^+}} ({\mathscr H} (\chi_*), \in $)). 
    
    For $ {\ell} = 1,2 $ let $ L^*_ {\ell} = L_{\mathbf{n} _ {\ell} }\cap \mathfrak{A}$ and $ \mathbf{n} ^*_{\ell} = \mathbf{n} _ {\ell} \upharpoonright L^*_{\ell} $, so by absoluteness $ \mathbb{P} _{\mathbf{n} ^*_{\ell}}  (L_{\mathbf{n} ^*_{\ell}}) = \mathbb{P} _{\mathbf{n} _{\ell} }( L_{\mathbf{n}^* _{\ell} })$ hence  $ \mathbb{P} _{\mathbf{n} ^*_{\ell} }(L_{\mathbf{n} ^*_{\ell} })  \lessdot \mathbb{P} _{\mathbf{n} _{\ell} }(L_{\mathbf{n} _{\ell} })$.
    By the choice of $ \mathbf{n} $ as very wide and full (see Definition \ref{c39}), also $\mathbf{n} \upharpoonright (\mathfrak{A} \cap L_ \mathbf{n} )$ is very wide and full of cardinality $ \chi  $. But we have  $ \mathbf{n} \upharpoonright (\mathfrak{A} \cap L_ \mathbf{n} ) 
    \le \mathbf{n} _2 \upharpoonright (\mathfrak{A} \cap L_ {\mathbf{n}_2} ) $   both of cardinality $ \chi $ hence  also $ \mathbf{n} ^*_2 $   is very wide  and full (see Definition \ref{c4}) of cardinality $ \chi$.  Now  easily $ g $ can be extended to an automorphism of  $\mathbf{n} ^*_2 $. The promised statement now follows.]
    
    Second, 
     
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_5$]  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})  \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    [Why? By\footnote{Can repeat the proof of $(*)_4 $  but for variety we give another proof.} the definitions and the induction hypothesis ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2} (L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1}) \subseteq  {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$ as quasi orders.  
    
    Also if $p_1,p_2 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})$ are compatible in
    ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$ let $q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$  be a common upper bound there.  We can find an $E_{\mathbf n_2}$-closed $L' \subseteq  L_{\mathbf n_1}$ of cardinality $\le \lambda_2$ (recalling $\mathbf n \in {\mathscr X} \Rightarrow |L_{\mathbf n}| \le
    \lambda_2$) such that $p_1,p_2 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_1}(L')$ and  $E_{\mathbf n_2}$-closed $L'' \subseteq L_{{\mathbf n}_{1}}$ of cardinality $\le \lambda_2$ such that $L' \subseteq L''$ and $q \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L'')$. Now we can find $f_1 \in {\mathscr F}$ such that ${\rm dom}(f_1) = \cup\{t/E_{\mathbf n_2}:t \in L'\} \cup M_{{\mathbf m}}$ recalling that $t/E_{\mathbf m} \supseteq M_{\mathbf m}$, see \ref{c5}(0) and $f_1$ is the identity. Then by $(*)_3$ we can find $f_2 \in {\mathscr F}$ extending $f_1$ with ${\rm dom}(f_2) = \cup\{t/E_{\mathbf n_2}:t \in L''\}$ and ${\rm rang}(f_2) \backslash {\rm rang}(f_1) \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_1}$.  So recalling $(*)_4(b)$ applied to $f$ we have ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}
    \models ``(p_1 \le \hat f_2(q)) \wedge (p_2 \le
    \hat f_2(q))"$ and $\hat f_2(q) \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})$ recalling
    $(*)_4$.  So $p_1,p_2$ are compatible also in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})$.  
    Obviously, if $p_1,p_2 \in {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})$ are compatible in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1  }),$ say, $q$ witnesses, then
    $q$ is a common upper bound of  $p_1,p_2$ in ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2} (L_\gamma)$.
    
    So every antichain of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})$ is an antichain of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$.  Similarly to the above every maximal
    antichain of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1})$ is a maximal antichain of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$; similarly for the
    other direction.  So we are done.]
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_6$]  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_1}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1}) = {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma \cap L_{\mathbf n_1}) \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L_\gamma)$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    [Why?  We prove this by induction on $\gamma$, as in proving the Tarski-Vaught criterion is sufficient (we shall  elaborate  later in the proof of \ref{e35}, more specifically $\boxplus_4$ proves a similar statement in detail with weaker assumptions).]
    
    Hence (using $\gamma = |L_{\mathbf n_2}|^+$),
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_7$]  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_1} \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}$.
    \end{enumerate}
     
    Hence for every $L \subseteq L_{\mathbf n_1}$ by \ref{c28}(4)  we have ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_1}(L) = 
    {\mathbb P}_{\mathbf n_2}(L)$ as required for ${\mathbf n} \in {\mathbf M}_{{\rm ec}}$, see Definition \ref{c34}.

    Let ${\mathbb P}$ be a forcing notion and $Y \subseteq {\mathbb P}$ and $\chi$ a regular cardinal.
    
    1) Let ${\mathbb L}_\chi(Y)$ be the set of sentences formed from $\{p:p \in {\mathbb P}\}$ closing under the operations $\neg p$ and $\bigwedge\limits_{i < \alpha} p_i$, for $\alpha < \chi$; so (infinitary) propositional logic.
    
    2) For a directed  $\mathbf G \subseteq {\mathbb P}$ and $\psi \in {\mathbb L}_\chi(Y)$ we define
    the truth value $\psi[\mathbf G]$ naturally (by induction on $\psi$ starting with $p[\mathbf G] = {\rm true} \Leftrightarrow p \in \mathbf G$).
    
    3) Let ${\mathbb L}^+_\chi(Y,{\mathbb P})$, the ${\mathbb L}_\chi$-closure of $Y$ for ${\mathbb P}$, (where $Y \subseteq {\mathbb P}$; if $Y = {\mathbb P}$ we may omit $Y$) be the following partial order:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$\bullet$]   set of elements $\{\psi \in {\mathbb L}_\chi(Y,{\mathbb P}): \, \nVdash_{{\mathbb P}} ``\psi[\let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\mathbf G$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}] =$ false"$\},$
        
        \item[$\bullet$]  the order $\psi_1 \le \psi_2$ iff $\Vdash_{{\mathbb P}}$ ``if $\psi_2[\let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-

    \end{enumerate}
    
    4) The completion of ${\mathbb P}$ is the ${\mathbb L}_\chi$-closure of ${\mathbb P}$ which is  ${\mathbb L}_\chi^{+}({\mathbb P})= \mathbb{L} ^+_\chi (\mathbb{P}, \mathbb{P} )$  where $\chi$ is minimal such that ${\mathbb P}$ satisfies the $\chi$-c.c.

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{b8}
    For a cardinal $\chi$ and forcing notion ${\mathbb P}$ and $Y \subseteq {\mathbb P}$ we have:
    
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  ${\mathbb L}^+_\chi(Y,{\mathbb P})$ is a forcing notion, 
        
        \item[(b)]  ${\mathbb P} \lessdot {\mathbb L}^+_\chi({\mathbb P})$ under the natural identification\footnote{Pedantically ${\mathbb P} \lessdot' {\mathbb L}^+_{\chi_{1}}[{\mathbb P}]$, see \ref{b11}(8), because ${\mathbb L}^+_\chi[{\mathbb P}] \models ``p \le q"$ {\underline{iff}} \, $q \Vdash_{{\mathbb P}} ``p \in \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\mathbf G$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{{\mathbb P}}"$.},
        
        \item[(c)]  ${\mathbb L}^+_\chi(Y,{\mathbb P}) \lessdot {\mathbb L}^+_\chi({\mathbb P})$, 
        
        \item[(d)]  ${\mathbb L}^+_{\chi_1}(Y,{\mathbb P}) \lessdot {\mathbb L}^+_{\chi_2}(Y,{\mathbb P})$ when $\chi_1 \le \chi_2$ are regular, 
        
        \item[(e)]  if ${\mathbb P}$ satisfies the $\chi_1$-c.c. and $\chi_1 < \chi_2$ are regular, {\underline{then}} \, ${\mathbb L}^+_{\chi_1}(Y,{\mathbb P})$ is essentially equal to ${\mathbb L}^+_{\chi_2}(Y,{\mathbb P})$, i.e. up to the natural equivalence of elements in a quasi order, 
        
        \item[(f)]  if $Y = {\mathbb P}$ then ${\mathbb P}$ is a dense subset of ${\mathbb L}^+_\chi({\mathbb P})$.
    \end{enumerate}

traightforward (recalling \ref{b29}(4)), i.e.
    
    1) By (2). 
    
    2) By (3) and (4).
    
    3) Obvious, see \ref{b14}(8).
    
    4) Clear.
    
    5) Easy.
     
    6) Choose $ \bar{c} $ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_1$]  
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)]  $ \bar{ c } \in {}^{ \delta } (M_ \mathbf{m})$   for some ordinal $ \delta $,
            
            \item[(b)] if $ \alpha < \beta < \delta $ then $c_ \beta \not\le_{M }  c_ \alpha $, 
            
            \item[(c)] $\bar{ c }$ lists $M_ \mathbf{m}$,
            
            \item[(d)] (follows),  if $ L \subseteq L_ \mathbf{m} $ has cardinality $ \le \lambda $ then for some $ \alpha < \delta $  the element $ c_ \alpha $ is an upper bound of $ L $, moreover $ L \in {\mathscr P} _{\mathbf{m}, < c_ \alpha }$.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
    
      
    Now we choose fat bounded $\mathbf{m}_\alpha$ by induction on $\alpha \le \delta $ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(*)_2$] 
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[(a)]  $ \langle \mathbf{m}_ \beta: \beta \le \alpha \rangle $  is $ \le _ \mathbf{M} $-increasing continuous,
            
             
            \item[(b)] $ L_{\mathbf{m}_0 } = M$ and  $ u_{\mathbf{m}_0, s}  = M_{< s }, $ (hence $ {\mathscr P}_{\mathbf{m}_0, s }=  [u_{\mathbf{m}_0, s }]^{\le \lambda }$ recalling ${\mathbf m}_{0}$ being fat) for $ s \in M$,
            
             
            \item[(c)]  for every $ s \in L_{ \mathbf{m}_ \alpha } \setminus M$  for some $\beta < \alpha $ we have $ L_{\mathbf{m}_ \alpha } \models s \le c_ \beta $,
            
             
            \item[(d)] if $ \gamma \in [ \alpha, \delta ) $ then  $ u_{\mathbf{m} _ \alpha,  c_\gamma}  =  L_{\mathbf{m} _ \alpha , < c_ \gamma }$,  
            
             
            \item[(e)]  if $ \alpha = \beta + 1 $ then $\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}(< c_ \beta) \in \mathbf{M} _{{\rm ec}},$
            
            \item[(f)] $L_ {\mathbf{m} _ \alpha }$ has cardinality at most $ 2^{ \lambda _2}$  or even $ \lambda _2 $,  but this does not matter, 
            
            \item[(g)] if $ t \in L_{\mathbf{m} _ \alpha} $ then for some  $\beta < \alpha $ we have  $ t/ E''_{\mathbf{m} _ \alpha } \subseteq L_{\mathbf{m} _{\beta + 1}}  \setminus L_{{\mathbf m}_{\beta}}.$  
        \end{enumerate} 
    \end{enumerate} 
    
    There is no problem to carry the definition; as:
    
    For $ \alpha = 0 $ we have defined $ \mathbf{m} _0$ in clause (b) of $(*)_2$ above.
    
    For $\alpha $ a limit ordinal use \ref{c28}(1), so in particular $L_{\mathbf{m}} =  \cup \{ L_{\mathbf{m}_ \beta }: \beta < \alpha\} $.  
    
    For $ \alpha = \beta + 1 $  by \ref{c41}  there is $ \mathbf{n} _ \beta \in \mathbf{M} _{{\rm ec}}$  such that $ \mathbf{m} _ \beta( < c_\beta)   \le_ \mathbf{M} \mathbf{n} _ \beta $,   {\rm without loss of generality} \, we have $ L_{\mathbf{m}_ \beta }  \cap L_{\mathbf{n}_ \beta }= L_{\mathbf{m}( < c_\beta)}$.

    By \ref{e37} below {\rm without loss of generality} \,  the cardinality of $ L_ {\mathbf{n} _ \beta} $  is at most $ \lambda _2$. Now apply \ref{b44}(3)  with $ \mathbf{m} _ \beta , L_{\mathbf{m} _\beta , < c_ \beta}, \mathbf{n}_\beta$   here standing for  $ \mathbf{m} _2, L_*, \mathbf{m}_1$ there.  

    So we have carried the induction. Now clearly $ \mathbf{m} _ \delta $ is as promised,  That is, $ (*)_{\mathbf{m} _\delta }$ from part (2) of the claim holds,  hence $ \mathbf{m} \in \mathbf{M} _{{\rm ec}}$ by part (2) being cofinal holds by \ref{c37};  so we are done.

\label{e10}
    Assume $\mathbf m$ is $ \mu $-wide where $ \mu \ge \lambda_{0}.$
    
     
    1) If $f \in {\mathscr F}_{{\mathbf m}, \mu }$ and $X \subseteq L_{\mathbf m}$ has cardinality
    $< \mu,$  {\underline{then}} \, there is $g$ such that:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  $g \in {\mathscr F}_{{\mathbf m}, \infty}$ and even belongs  to $ {\mathscr F} _{\mathbf{m}, \mu }$,
        
        \item[(b)]  $f \subseteq g$, 
        
        \item[(c)]  ${\rm dom}(g) = {\rm rang}(g)$,  
        
        \item[(d)]  $X \subseteq {\rm dom}(g)$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    2) If $g \in {\mathscr F}_{\mathbf m, \mu }$  and ${\rm dom}(g) = {\rm rang}(g)$ {\underline{then}} \, $g^{+ \mathbf m} = g \cup {\rm id}_{L_{\mathbf m} \backslash {\rm dom}(g)}$ is an automorphism of $\mathbf m$.
    
    3) If $f$ is an automorphism of $\mathbf m$ {\underline{then}} \, it naturally induces an automorphism $\hat f$ of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_{\mathbf m})$ similarly to $\hat f$ from $(*)_4(b)$ of the proof of \ref{c41} and it induces an automorphism of $ \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} [L_ \mathbf{m} ]$ as well; abusing our notation we denote both by  $ \hat{f}.$
    
    4) If $f \in {\mathscr F}_{\mathbf m , \mu }$  {\underline{then}} \, it induces an isomorphism $\hat f$ from  $ \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} [{\rm dom} (f)]$  onto  $ \mathbb{P} _ \mathbf{m} [{\rm rang}(f)]$  hence (as above) from

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{e24}
    Assume $\mathbf m \in \mathbf M$.
    
    1) Let ${\mathscr Y}_{\mathbf m}$ be the set of pairs $(t,\bar s)$ such that  $t \in L_{\mathbf m} \backslash M_{\mathbf m}$ and $\bar s \in 
    {}^\zeta(t/E''_{\mathbf m})$ for some $\zeta < \lambda^+$;  we may write $\bar s$ instead of $(t,\bar s)$  as usually $\bar s$ determines $t/E''_ \mathbf{m} $,  but this is the only information  about $t$  that matter.  We could have used instead pairs  $ (t/E''_\mathbf{m} , \bar{s})$.
          
    2)  By induction on the ordinal $\gamma$ we define when  $(t_1,\bar s_1),(t_2,\bar s_2)$ are $\gamma$-equivalent in $\mathbf m$ or are $(\mathbf m,\gamma)$-equivalent:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  if $\gamma=0$, {\underline{then}} \, letting $L_\ell = (M_{\mathbf m} \cup {\rm rang}(\bar s_\ell))$ for $\ell=1,2$ there is $h$ such that: 
        
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item[$(\alpha)$]  $h$ is an isomorphism from $\mathbf m {\restriction} L_1$ onto $\mathbf m {\restriction} L_2$, 
            
            \item[$(\beta)$]  $h$ maps $\bar s_1$ to $\bar s_2$,
            
            \item[$(\gamma)$]  $h {\restriction} M_{\mathbf m}$ is the identity,
            
            \item[$(\delta)$]  $h$ induces an isomorphism from  ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$ onto ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_2)$ (as defined in \ref{c4}$(*)_4(b)$),  
            
            \item[$(\varepsilon)$]  moreover, $h$ induces an isomorphism from ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}[L_1]$ onto ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}[L_2]$, as defined in \ref{b20}, so $p^*_{t,\eta} \mapsto p^*_{h(t),\eta}$, see \ref{b11}(3), 
        \end{enumerate}
        
        \item[(b)]  if $\gamma = \beta +1$ {\underline{then}} \, for every  $\ell \in \{1,2\}$ for every 
        $\varepsilon < \lambda^+$ and  $\bar s'_\ell \in {}^\varepsilon(t_\ell/E''_{\mathbf m})$  there is  $\bar s'_{3 - \ell} \in {}^\varepsilon(t_{3 - \ell}/E''_{\mathbf m})$ such that $(t_1,\bar s_1 \char 94 \bar s'_1),(t_2,\bar s_2 \char 94 \bar s'_2)$ are $\beta$-equivalent, 
        
        \item[(c)]  if $\gamma$ is a limit ordinal {\underline{then}} \, $(t_1,\bar s_1), (t_2,\bar s_2)$ are $\beta$-equivalent for every $\beta < \gamma$.
    \end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
y induction on $\alpha$.
    
     
    \underline{Case 1}:  $\alpha = 0$:
    
    Note that the set of elements of ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(M_{\mathbf m} \cup {\rm rang}(\bar s))$ has cardinality $\le 2^{\lambda_1}$ (and even $\le
    (\lambda_1)^\lambda$) and depends just on $\mathbf m {\restriction} (M_{\mathbf m} \cup {\rm rang}(\bar s))$ but there are $\beth_2(\lambda_1)$  possibilities for the quasi order on ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}(L_1)$ and even for ${\mathbb P}_{\mathbf m}[L_1]$.  
    
    \underline{Case 2}:  $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal:
    
    By clause (c) of Definition \ref{e24}, the number of $\alpha$-equivalence classes is $\le \prod\limits_{\beta < \alpha}$ (the
    number of $\beta$-equivalence classes) 
    $\le \prod\limits_{\beta < \alpha} \beth_{1 + \beta +1} (\lambda_1) \le  (\beth_{1 + \alpha +1}(\lambda_1))^{\beth_{1 + \alpha}} = 
    \beth_{1 + \alpha +1}(\lambda_1)$.
    
    \underline{Case 3}:  $\alpha = \beta +1$:
    
    Clearly every $\alpha$-equivalence class can be coded as a set of $\beta$-equivalence classes hence the number of $\alpha$-equivalence
    classes is $\le 2^{\beth_{1 + \beta +1}(\lambda_1)}  = \beth_{1 + \beta +2}(\lambda_1) = \beth_{1 + \alpha +1}(\lambda_1)$, as promised.

label: g5
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{g5}
    Assume ${\mathbf m} \in {\mathbf M}, M \subseteq M_{{\mathbf m}}$ and $\mathscr{L} \subseteq \rm{cmp}(M, {\mathbf m}).$

    1) We define $\rm{rest}(\mathscr{L}, M, {\mathbf m})$ as  the object ${\mathbf n}$ consisting of (intended to be in ${\mathbf M}$):
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] the set of elements of $L_{{\mathbf n}}$ is $\bigcup \{ L: L \in \mathscr{L} \} \cup M,$
        
        \item[(b)] the order on $L_{{\mathbf m}}$ is $<_{{\mathbf m}} {\restriction} L_{{\mathbf n}},$
        
        \item[(c)] $M_{{\mathbf n}} = M,$
        
        \item[(d)] $E_{{\mathbf n}}' = E_{{\mathbf m}}' {\restriction} L_{{\mathbf n}},$
        
        \item[(e)] $u_{{\mathbf n}, s} = u_{{\mathbf m}, s} \cap L_{{\mathbf n}},$
        
        \item[(f)] ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, s} = {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, s} \cap [u_{{\mathbf n}, s}]^{\leq \lambda}.$
    \end{enumerate}

    2) Further assume ${\mathbf m} \in {\mathbf M}_{\leq \lambda_{2}}.$ We define $\rm{Rest}(\mathscr{L}, M, {\mathbf m})$ as the object ${\mathbf n}$ consisting of (intended to be in ${\mathbf M}$):

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] $L_{{\mathbf n}} = L_{{\mathbf m}},$
        
        \item[(b)] $M_{{\mathbf n}} = M,$
        
        \item[(c)] $E_{{\mathbf n}}' = \{ (s_{1}, s_{2}): \text{for some} \ L \in \mathscr{L}, (s_{1}, s_{2}) \in E_{{\mathbf m}}' {\restriction} L \ \text{\underline{or}} \ (\forall L \in \mathscr{L})({s_{1}, s_{2} \notin L \setminus M}), \\ \{s_{1}, s_{2} \} \subseteq L_{{\mathbf n}}, \{ s_{1}, s_{2} \} \nsubseteq M_{{\mathbf n}} \},$
        
        \item[(d)] $u_{{\mathbf n}, s} = u_{{\mathbf m}, s}$ for $s \in L_{{\mathbf n}},$
        
        \item[(e)] ${\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf n}, s} = {\mathscr P}_{{\mathbf m}, s}.$
    \end{enumerate}

    3) We may omit $\mathscr{L}$ when $\mathscr{L} = \rm{cmp}(M, {\mathbf m}).$
    
    4) For ${\mathbf r} \in {\mathbf R},$ let $\Xi_{{\mathbf r}}^{\bullet}$ be the set of $\bar{\nu}$ such that some ${\mathbf G}^{\bullet}$ witness it, which means:
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] ${\mathbf G}^{\bullet} \subseteq {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}} \cap N_{{\mathbf r}}$ is generic over $N_{{\mathbf r}},$
        
        \item[(b)] $\bar{\nu} = \langle \nu_{s}: s \in M_{{\mathbf m}} \cap N_{{\mathbf r}} \rangle,$
        
        \item[(c)] $\nu_{s} = \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\eta$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}_{s}[{\mathbf G}^{\bullet}]$ for $s \in M_{{\mathbf m}} \cap N_{{\mathbf r}}.$  
    \end{enumerate}
    
    (So compared to Definition \ref{e53}(2B) clause (c)($\gamma$) is not required here). 
    
    5) For ${\mathbf r} \in \mathbf{R}, M' \subseteq M_{{\mathbf m}}$ such that $ M' \in N_{{\mathbf r}}$ and $ M = M' \cap N_{{\mathbf r}},$ let $\Xi_{M}^{\bullet} = \Xi_{{\mathbf r}, M}^{\bullet}$ be the set of $\bar{\nu} = \langle \nu_{s}: s \in M \rangle$ such that some pair $({\mathbf n}, {\mathbf G})$ witnesses $\bar{\nu}$ which means: 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(\alpha)$]  ${\mathbf n} \leq_{{\mathbf M}} \rm{rest}(M', {\mathbf m})$ and ${\mathbf n} \in N_{{\mathbf r}}$ and ${\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf n}} \lessdot {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}},$
        
        \item[$(\beta)$] ${\mathbf G}$ is a subset of ${\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf n}} \cap N_{{\mathbf r}}$ generic over $N_{{\mathbf r}},$
        
        \item[$(\gamma)$] $\nu_{s} = \let\theaccent\tilde\skewfactor-
\mathpalette\oalign{$3\eta_{s}$\cr\hidewidth
\vbox to.2ex{\hbox{$3\skew\skewfactor\theaccent{}$}\vss}\hidewidth}[{\mathbf G}]$ for $s \in M.$
    \end{enumerate}

label: g8

body_md:
\label{g8}
    Assume ${\mathbf m} \in {\mathbf M}, M \subseteq M_{{\mathbf m}},$  $\mathscr{L} \subseteq \rm{cmp}(M, {\mathbf m}),$ ${{\mathbf n}_{2}} := \rm{Rest}(\mathscr{L}, M, {\mathbf m})$ (see \ref{g5}(2)) and ${\mathbf n}_{1} = \rm{rest}(\mathscr{L}, M, {\mathbf m}),$ (see \ref{g5}(1)):
    
    1) ${\mathbf n}_{1} \leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\mathbf n}_{2},$ 
    
    2) $L_{{\mathbf n}_{2}} = L_{{\mathbf m}}, {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf n}_{2}} = {\mathbb P}_{{\mathbf m}}$ and $\rm{cmp}(M, {\mathbf n}_{1}) = \mathscr{L} \subseteq {\rm cmp}(M, {\mathbf n}_{2})$ and ${\rm cmp}(M, {\mathbf n}_{2}) \setminus {\mathscr{L}}$ is empty or a singleton; note that this is the single $E_{{\mathbf n}_{2}}'$-class that is not in ${\mathscr{L}}_{{\mathbf n}_{1}}.$
    
    3) If $M = M_{{\mathbf m}}$ and ${\mathscr{L}} = {\rm cmp}(M, {\mathbf m})$ then ${\mathbf n}_{1} = {\mathbf n}_{2} = {\mathbf m}.$
     
    4) if $\iota \in \{1, 2 \}$ and ${\mathbf n}_{\iota} \leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\mathbf n}_{*}$ and $L_{{\mathbf n}_{*}} \cap L_{{\mathbf m}} = L_{{\mathbf n}_{\iota}},$ \underline{then} we can find ${\mathbf m}_{*}$ such that: 
    
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] ${\mathbf m} \leq_{{\mathbf M}} {\mathbf m}_{*}$ and $L_{{\mathbf m}_{*}} = L_{{\mathbf n}_{*}} \cup L_{{\mathbf m}},$
        
        \item[(b)] $\mathscr{L} \subseteq \rm{cmp}(M, {\mathbf m}_{*}),$
        
        \item[(c)] if $\iota = 2$ then  $ {\mathbf n}_{*} = \rm{Rest}(\mathscr{L}, M, {\mathbf m}_{*}),$
        
        \item[(d)] if $\iota = 1 $ letting $\mathscr{L}_{1} = \rm{cmp}(M, {\mathbf n}_{*})$ we have ${\mathbf n}_{*} = \rm{rest}(\mathscr{L}_{1}, M, {\mathbf m}_{*}),$
        
        \item[(e)] (choosing minimal $u$) if $t \in M_{{\mathbf m}} \setminus M$ and $\iota = 1,$ then $u_{{\mathbf m}_{*}, t} = u_{{\mathbf m}, t} \cup \{ s: s \in L_{{\mathbf n}_{*}} \setminus L_{{\mathbf m}}  \ s \in u_{{\mathbf n}, t} \}.$ 
    \end{enumerate}
